questions.prompt: `./prog a b c` is run. What are `argc` and `argv[2]`?
questions.explain: `argv[0]` is the program name, so there are 4 entries: `./prog`, `a`, `b`, `c`. `argv[2]` is `"b"`.
option_notes: argc counts the program name too.

questions.prompt: Which `main` signature also receives the environment variables?
options: int main(int argc, char *argv[], int envc)
questions.explain: Unix (as a common extension) passes a third parameter, a NULL-terminated array of `"NAME=value"` strings. `getenv("NAME")` is the portable way to read one variable.
C passes arguments by value: `swap` receives copies of `x` and `y`, swaps the copies and the caller's variables are unchanged. To change them you must pass their addresses.
option_notes: Correct: the swap only happens inside the function.
That would need `swap(&x, &y)` and pointer parameters.
Nothing assigns the same value to both.

questions.prompt: `char buf[10];` Which calls can NEVER write past the end of `buf`?
questions.explain: `fgets` takes the buffer size; `%9s` limits scanf to 9 characters plus the terminator. `gets` and an unbounded `%s` read as much as the user types (this is why `gets` was removed from C11).
option_notes: Bounded by the size you pass.

questions.prompt: `scanf` needs the {{0}} of the variable to store the value in, which is why you write `scanf("%d", &n)`.
questions.explain: `&n` is a pointer to `n`; scanf writes the converted value through it.

questions.prompt: The `printf` conversion to print a `size_t` is `%{{0}}`.
questions.explain: `%zu` is the length modifier `z` (size_t) with the conversion `u` (unsigned). Using `%d` for a `size_t` is a bug on 64-bit systems.
`fgets` keeps the newline in the buffer and always adds the terminating `'\0'`. That is why programs often strip it with `line[strcspn(line, "\n")] = '\0'`.

questions.prompt: Put these in the order the compiler needs to see them for a function defined after `main`.
items: Prototype: int media(int a, int b);
Definition: int media(int a, int b) { ... }
questions.explain: A call must be preceded by at least a declaration (prototype) so the compiler knows the argument and return types. The definition can come later in the file or in another file.
